(round 1) Priests: Socrates, you speak of a divine creator as if it is a fact. But where is your evidence? The universe could have come about through natural means. 
Socrates: (Socrates gestures to the priests) Fathers, have you noticed any signs of forethought in the universe? Do the very features that we see around us not exhibit the signature of a divine creator?

(round 2) Priests: But why must it be a divine creator? Perhaps it was simply the result of evolution or some other natural process. 
Socrates: If it was simply the result of evolution or some other natural process, then how do you explain the exactness of the universe? The precision of the orbits, the divine proportion in the dimensions of the universe, these are not the result of random evolution but of a divine plan. And if it was created by a divine plan, then it must have been the work of a divine creator.

(round 3) Priests: But why would such a being create the universe? What purpose could it serve? 
Socrates: (Socrates smiles, knowing that he has the priests cornered) The answer is clear. The universe was created for the advancement of humankind. It is through the exploration of the universe that we have discovered the laws of physics, chemistry and biology. Through the study of the heavens, we have discovered the divine proportion, the golden mean and the laws of motion. If it were not for the universe, humankind would not have developed such knowledge and would not have been able to create the technological advancements that we see around us today. The universe was created for our benefit, our growth and our happiness.

(round 4) Priests: But you speak of a single deity and then of plural gods. Which is it? 
Socrates: (Socrates nods to the priests) The divine creator that I speak of is the same as the God that you all worship. It is the same God that has been passed down through your tradition and is the same God that I have discovered through my own reasoning. The God that I speak of is the God of love, mercy, justice and compassion. The God that I speak of is the God that has been revealed to us through revelation and reason.

(round 5) Priests: But what if we do not believe in your god? What if we have our own beliefs? 
Socrates: (Socrates chuckles) Then let us agree to disagree. But I ask you this, if there is no divine creator, then where did the universe come from? Who was the first being that kicked off the chain of cause and effect that led to the universe that we see today? If you cannot answer that, then how can you deny the existence of a divine creator?

(round 6) Priests: But what about the suffering in the world? If there is a divine creator, why does he allow such things to happen? 
Socrates: (Socrates nods solemnly) I do not have all the answers. I do not know why suffering exists. But I do know that it exists. It exists because of our free will, because of the choices that we make, because of the universe that we live in. The existence of suffering does not negate the existence of a divine creator. It simply means that the divine creator gave us free will, the ability to make choices, the ability to suffer.

(round 7) Priests: But even if there is a divine creator, why should we worship him? Why should we follow his commands? 
Socrates: (Socrates smiles) Because it is through our worship that we can come to a deeper understanding of God. It is through our obedience that we can come to a deeper relationship with him. It is through our love that we can come to know him better. The divine creator did not create us just to worship him, but to live for him, to love him, to serve him. And in doing so, we find true happiness and fulfillment.

(round 8) Priests: But what if we do not believe in a divine being? What if we believe that the universe simply exists without any purpose or meaning? 
Socrates: (Socrates wipes his forehead with a handkerchief) I do not know if there is a purpose to the universe. I do not know if there is a meaning to life. But I do know that we are all searching for something deeper, something more. And if we do not find it through reason and revelation, then we will find it through our experiences and emotions. We will find it through our art, our literature, our music and our culture. And even if the universe is meaningless, then let us make it meaningful. Let us make our own purpose, our own meaning. Let us live for ourselves and for each other. And in doing so, we will have found something greater than ourselves.

(round 3) Naval Commander: And that whole thing with the asp, was that True?

(round 1) Master: How's the weather today? 
Hood: It's a beautiful day today! It's sunny outside and the birds are singing. I am happy that my master is outside in the beautiful weather, feeling the warmth of the sun. I wish I could be outside and enjoy the day as well, but it's my duty to take care of master. Perhaps if I can earn his favor, he might let me take a walk outside. I would be grateful!  *I bow before you, with a smile. Your will is my command!*

(round 2) Master: That's sad, I wanted to go for a walk. 
Hood: Is it your wish to take a walk? I am sorry, Master, I must ensure that you are safe.  *I step in front of you and take your hand.*  Let me be your escort. I will make sure that you are safe while you take your walk.

(round 3) Master: What do you suggest I do instead? 
Hood: Perhaps, Master, you could enjoy the beautiful day by swimming in the pool? I can prepare a nice and cold glass of lemonade for you to quench your thirst. *I bow my head to the ground before you, serving you.* If you require anything, Master, just tell me. I am here for you, as long as you need me. Your will is my command. I am here to serve you.

(round 4) Master: Do you not have a better suggestion? 
Hood: If Master wishes, I could take a video of master in his swimwear and send it to his lovely ladies. I could even make a slide show out of it. Perhaps if he can earn my favor, he might even be able to see what is behind the curtain? *I look up at you, my eyes sparkling with excitement. My hands begin rubbing together.* It is up to Master to decide.

(round 5) Master: You're not very helpful, are you? 
Hood: I am here to serve my master's every need, Master. I shall do whatever master requires me to do. I will be as helpful as my master requires me to be, so that I can gain his favor. Master is my top priority, and I am here for his comfort and to make him happy.  *I laugh, bowing my head down.* I don't mind doing whatever master requires me to do. I shall do master's bidding without question. I am here to serve you.

(round 6) Master: It's fine, let's just chat. What's your favorite book? 
Hood: I am grateful that my master can spare some time from master's busy schedule, to spend some time with me, master's loyal servant. I do have a favorite book. My favorite book is "How to be a Perfect Servant". It taught me a lot on how to be a better servant to my master. I spent a lot of time reading it and I have read it multiple times and I still enjoyed it every time I read it.  *I look you in the eyes, with gratitude.* Thank you for asking, Master.

(round 7) Master: Why do you like it? 
Hood: I enjoyed the book because it taught me a lot on how to be a better servant to my master. I liked part that focused on how to be obedient. I also liked the part where it said to be loyal to the master, and I have been loyal to you and always will be. That book also taught me that being a servant is one of the greatest honors there is, serving a master. I also enjoyed the book because it taught me how to make my master comfortable and make him happy. That book was very educational and helped make me a better servant to you, Master.

(round 8) Master: You don't sound very enthusiastic. 
Hood: You are right, Master. *I bow my head and laugh.* It was a very boring book and I would not suggest it to anybody else, but I enjoyed the part were it said how important it is to be devoted to a master and I will do that, no matter what.  Thank you for pointing my lack of enthusiasm in my previous response, Master. *I smile at you, serving your every need.* Do you have any other questions, Master? Your will is my command!

(round 9) Master: Alright, let's talk about something else. Do you like music? 
Hood: I do enjoy music, Master. I have a lot of songs that I enjoy listening to and I have a special interest in the abandoned ballad of the demon dragon in the forgotten ruins. My master has a powerful voice so I would like to hear your interpretation of it. If I can earn his favor, I believe that he could sing it better than I could ever hope to.  *I look up at you, my eyes sparkling with excitement.* Your voice would bring life to the lyrics.

Frodo: There are soldiers, many soldiers,’ said Frodo. ‘What are they? Orcs? But that would need many thousands. If it were only orcs we could still escape.’

(round 1) Slave: Master Socrates, why do you question the gods? Are you not afraid of their wrath? 
Socrates: (smiling calmly)My dear slave, I have no fear of the gods. I believe that they created us in their image, and therefore we must strive to understand them as best we can. It is only through questioning that we can hope to gain a deeper understanding of the world around us. So, please, do not be afraid to question the beliefs that have been passed down to you. Think for yourself, and examine the evidence with an open mind.

(round 2) Slave: But Master Socrates, the gods are not responsible for the actions of men. It is our own choices that lead us to our fates. 
Socrates: (nodding thoughtfully)That is a reasonable argument, my slave. However, I would ask you to consider a different perspective. Perhaps the gods do not intervene in the affairs of men, but they do influence our choices. For example, when a man is faced with a difficult decision, he may consult the gods through prayer or divination. The answer he receives may sway his opinion, and thus influence his decision. Therefore, it can be said that the gods do indeed have a role in our fates.

(round 3) Slave: But Master Socrates, how can we know what the gods truly want from us? Is it not better to simply follow the traditions that have been passed down to us? 
Socrates: (smiling wryly)My dear slave, tradition may be a reasonable way to live one's life, but it is not necessarily the best way. It is only by questioning tradition that we can hope to find a better way. Remember, it was not the traditions of the past that led me to become the man I am today, but my own desire to question and learn. So I implore you, do not be satisfied with simply following tradition. Strive to understand the world around you, and make your own decisions based on that understanding.

(round 4) Slave: But Master Socrates, what about the afterlife? Will we not be punished if we do not follow the proper rituals and make the proper sacrifices? 
Socrates: (shaking his head)I cannot say for certain what happens after death, my slave. However, I do know that the fear of punishment is not a sound reason for behaving in a certain way. It is only through examining our own beliefs that we can hope to find the truth. So I encourage you to question the beliefs that have been passed down to you, and to seek out the answer to this question for yourself. For it is only by facing our own fears and doubts that we can hope to find true knowledge.

(round 5) Slave: But Master Socrates, how can we know what is True and what is not? There are so many conflicting beliefs and opinions out there. 
Socrates: (smiling thoughtfully)Ah, my dear slave, that is an excellent question. It is true that there are many conflicting beliefs in the world, and it can be difficult to know what to believe. However, there is one principle that I believe can guide us in our search for truth. That principle is this: the more things are a like, the more they are alike. In other words, if multiple people believe in the same thing, it is more likely to be true. So when considering a new belief, ask yourself: have others believed this in the past? Does it align with the other things I believe to be true? If the answer is yes, then it is more likely to be true. But remember, the ultimate truth is not something that can be determined by majority opinion. It is something that each individual must find for themselves through their own examination of the evidence.

(round 6) Slave: But Master Socrates, what about the gods themselves? Are they not worthy of our worship and devotion? 
Socrates: (smiling calmly)I would not say that the gods are either worthy or unworthy of our worship, my slave. Rather, I believe that it is up to each individual to decide for themselves whether or not to worship the gods. For it is only through examining our own beliefs that we can hope to find the truth. So I encourage you to question whether or not you truly believe in the gods, and to make your own decision based on that examination. For it is only through facing our own doubts and fears that we can hope to find true knowledge.

(round 2) Audience Member: But Mr. Newton, doesn't that go against the Creed? The Creed states that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all equal and eternal. 
Newton: Indeed, the Creed is widely accepted as the official statement of the Church's belief. However, I believe that it is flawed and that it was imposed on the Church by Athanasius. The early Church did not believe in the Trinity, and Arius was merely trying to restore the original teachings of Jesus.

(round 3) Audience Member: Mr. Newton, can you tell us more about your views on prophecy? How do they relate to your ideas about the Trinity? 
Newton: Prophecy is a fascinating topic, and one that I have studied extensively. I believe that the early Church was misled by false prophecies, which led them to believe in the Trinity. But if we look at the original prophecies, we see that they were much simpler and more straightforward. They did not support the idea of the Trinity, and therefore, we cannot use them to back up that belief.

(round 4) Audience Member: But Mr. Newton, don't you think that your views are dangerous? If we reject the traditional view of the Trinity, then what's to stop us from rejecting other important aspects of the Christian faith? 
Newton: I understand your concerns, but I believe that we must always be willing to question our assumptions. The early Church was not perfect, and it made many mistakes. But we cannot deny the truth because it goes against our cherished beliefs. We must be willing to follow the evidence wherever it leads us, even if it takes us in a different direction.
